name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,373

entries.clue: Secured mobile in deal (6)

indicatorNotes.mobile: Something mobile is free to move around, so the letters it points at are free to move into a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A phone contract finally locked in, with a new mobile thrown into the deal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like a phone in the surface; here it only says the letters of IN DEAL are free to move.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the informal sense: to nail a deal or a win is to clinch it, make it fast.

entries.clue: Write about boxer from mountainous land (6)

indicatorNotes.about: To turn about is to face the other way, so the word it follows is written the other way round.

blocks.note: to pen = to write
reversal indicator: PEN becomes NEP
Muhammad Ali, the crossword's favourite boxer

annotation.surface: An instruction to write a profile of a fighter who hails from a mountain country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Write about boxer' reads as a journalist's assignment; 'about' is really turning PEN around. The definition is adjectival: Nepali means from Nepal, the Himalayan land.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: Nepal holds much of the Himalaya, and Nepali is its adjective, so 'from mountainous land' fits.

entries.clue: Hurt in martial art, almost holding on (7)

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost means not quite all of it, so the word loses its last letter.
indicatorNotes.holding: Holding means gripping something within, so the next piece goes inside this one.

blocks.note: taken as written
JUDO without its last letter, which 'almost' asks for
re = on, concerning, as in 'a report on/re the matter'; it goes inside JUD

annotation.surface: Someone got hurt doing a martial art, nearly managing to hang on.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a judo bout gone wrong. RE for 'on' is the memo-heading sense: 'on the subject of'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are past participles meaning harmed in body.

entries.clue: Name of woman rising in the morning with me (4)

indicatorNotes.rising: Rising means going up, and in a down entry going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards.

blocks.note: a.m. = in the morning
taken as written, placed 'with' the AM
reversal indicator: the joined letters are read upwards

annotation.surface: A woman who gets up in the morning alongside the speaker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rising in the morning' paints someone getting out of bed; in a down clue, rising means read upwards, so AM ME becomes EMMA.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the answer is one particular woman's first name, as in Jane Austen's heroine.

entries.clue: Healthcare worker they’d said regularly gets involved in back operation (6)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Regularly means at even intervals, so take every other letter of the words before it.
indicatorNotes.gets involved in: To get involved in something is to be drawn inside it, so these letters go inside the next piece.
indicatorNotes.back: Back means backwards, the direction you go when you go back, so the word is written in reverse.

blocks.note: every second letter of tHeYdSaId
OP, short for operation, written backwards; HYSI goes inside it

annotation.surface: A physiotherapist is drawn into an operation on someone's back, according to what they said.
annotation.walkthrough: The medical setting makes 'back operation' sound like spinal surgery; really it is OP turned back. Physio is the everyday short form of physiotherapist.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a physio (physiotherapist) is one kind of healthcare worker, treating injuries with exercise and massage.

entries.clue: Worker rejected untrustworthy person’s support (8)

indicatorNotes.rejected: To reject something is to send it back, so the word is sent back to front.

blocks.note: a hand = a worker, as in farmhand
a liar cannot be trusted
reversal indicator: LIAR becomes RAIL

annotation.surface: An employee turns down the backing of someone they don't trust.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as office politics; 'support' sounds like backing, but it is a physical rail you grip on stairs.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: a handrail is a rail you grip on stairs, there to support you.

entries.clue: Lifting, say, is exercise (3,2)

indicatorNotes.Lifting: Lifting means raising, and in a down entry raising letters means reading them from the bottom up, so they reverse.

blocks.note: to put = to say, as in 'to put it bluntly'
taken as written
reversal indicator: the joined letters are read upwards

annotation.surface: A claim that lifting weights, for example, counts as exercise.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lifting, say' reads as weightlifting given as an example; 'say' is really PUT, and 'Lifting' turns PUT IS upside down in this down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the sit-up, raising the trunk from lying flat, is one particular exercise for the stomach muscles.

entries.clue: On vacation, ordered food of dubious nature (6)

indicatorNotes.On vacation: A vacated room has been emptied, so on vacation the word is emptied of its middle, leaving only its outer letters.

blocks.note: ORDERED emptied, leaving its outer letters O and D
a dish = an item of food

annotation.surface: A holiday-maker orders a meal abroad and suspects it's not quite right.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' reads as a holiday; in crosswords it means a word is vacated, keeping only its outside letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: oddish means somewhat odd, a little questionable, which is what 'of dubious nature' describes.

entries.clue: Finally remedy hole in father’s nightwear (7)

indicatorNotes.Finally: Finally means at the very end, so take the last letter of the next word.
indicatorNotes.in: In means inside, so the letters before it are placed inside the word after it.

blocks.note: last letter of remedY
a hole = a jam, a tight spot, as in 'in a hole'
pa = father, plus the S; YJAM goes inside it

annotation.surface: A plea to mend the hole in Dad's pyjamas at last.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is darning, but 'hole' is a predicament, hence JAM. PYJAMAS is the British spelling of pajamas.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: pyjamas are the loose jacket and trousers worn in bed, the commonest nightwear.

entries.clue: Some Victorians and all Edwardians in lightweight footwear (9)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some means a portion of what follows, so the answer is a run of letters taken from inside those words.

blocks.note: the run starts at the last letter of Victorians and ends two letters into Edwardians

annotation.surface: A claim about period dress: a few Victorians, and every Edwardian, wore sandals.
annotation.walkthrough: The history-of-fashion surface hides the answer across four words: victorianS AND ALL EDwardians. Sandalled, with the double L, is the British spelling.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: sandals are light open shoes, so someone sandalled is in lightweight footwear.

entries.clue: Renowned editor finishing new books (5)

indicatorNotes.finishing: Finishing something means coming at its end, so this piece goes last.

blocks.note: n = new
OT = Old Testament, a set of books
ed = editor; it finishes the word

annotation.surface: A famous editor puts the last touches to some new books.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about publishing, so 'books' and 'editor' seem to belong together; here they are separate pieces, and 'finishing' just places ED at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a noted scholar and a renowned scholar are both widely known.

entries.clue: Bird left Noah’s vessel (4)

blocks.note: l = left
the boat Noah built for the flood

annotation.surface: A bird flew off from Noah's ark.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as a verb, the bird leaving the ark, which echoes the dove and raven Noah sent out; it is only the letter L.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the lark, famous for singing as it climbs, is one particular bird.

entries.clue: Ciphers gent uncovered beside underground chambers (8)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: Uncovered means with the covering stripped off, and a word's covering is its first and last letters.
indicatorNotes.beside: Beside means standing next to, so the two pieces are simply put side by side.

blocks.note: gENt without its outer letters
crypts are vaults beneath churches

annotation.surface: A man stripped bare next to some cellars, as if in a spy thriller full of codes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ciphers' looks like a plural noun, codes; it is a verb here, meaning puts into code.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: as verbs, to cipher a message and to encrypt it both mean to put it into code.

entries.clue: Insect hidden in ordinary fruit (8)

indicatorNotes.hidden in: Something hidden in a place is tucked inside it, so the first piece goes inside the second.

blocks.note: plain = ordinary; it is split to hold the insect
the crossword's standard insect; goes inside PLAIN

annotation.surface: A bug is concealed inside an unremarkable piece of fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hidden in' tempts a solver to look for letters running inside 'ordinary fruit'; here it puts ANT inside a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the plantain is a starchy banana-like fruit, usually eaten cooked.

entries.clue: Spotted dog close to field barking at animal (9)

indicatorNotes.close to: The close of something is its end, so take the last letter of the next word.
indicatorNotes.barking: Barking is British slang for mad, and mad letters are scrambled into a new order.

blocks.note: last letter of fielD
AT ANIMAL rearranged; 'barking' is the indicator

annotation.surface: A spotted dog near a field barks at some creature.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Barking' fits the dog perfectly, but it is British slang for mad, the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the Dalmatian is the breed marked all over with black or liver spots.

entries.clue: Dull Renault hybrid (7)

indicatorNotes.hybrid: A hybrid is a cross or mixture, so the letters of the word are mixed up.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A verdict on a hybrid Renault car: boring.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hybrid' reads as a petrol-electric car, which fits Renault, the French carmaker; it is really the mixing signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A near-synonym from colour: neutral shades such as beige and grey are muted, dull.

entries.clue: Lightly hit adept shot to gain lead in polo (6)

indicatorNotes.shot: Shot means wrecked, as in 'my nerves are shot', so the letters are broken up and rearranged.
indicatorNotes.to gain: To gain something is to take it on, so the next piece is added to the fodder before it is shuffled.
indicatorNotes.lead in: The lead is whoever goes first, so the lead in a word is its first letter.

blocks.note: anagram fodder
first letter of Polo, added to the fodder
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A skilled polo player gently strikes the ball to take the lead.
annotation.walkthrough: The polo surface makes 'shot' a stroke of the mallet; it means the letters of ADEPT plus P are shot to pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to tap is to strike lightly, and the past tense matches 'hit'.

entries.clue: Just married before end of financial year (6)

indicatorNotes.end of: The end of a word is its final letter, so take only that.

blocks.note: m = married, as in genealogies
ere = before, poetically
last letter of financiaL
y = year

annotation.surface: A couple wed just before the tax year closes, perhaps for the tax break.
annotation.walkthrough: 'End of financial year' reads as one accounting phrase; 'end of' takes only the L, and 'year' is a separate Y.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'just a child' and 'merely a child' both mean only, no more than.

entries.clue: Dispatched parts competently, without thinking (8)

indicatorNotes.parts: To part something is to split it open, as a curtain parts, so the other piece goes into the gap.

blocks.note: ably = competently; it is split to hold SENT
sent = dispatched; goes inside ABLY

annotation.surface: Someone shipped out machine parts efficiently but mindlessly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Parts' reads as a noun, spare parts in a warehouse; it is a verb, SENT parting ABLY.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiomatic synonym: doing something absently means your mind is absent, so you do it without thinking.

entries.clue: Blemish on female’s neck covering (5)

indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry, one thing on another sits above it, so the first piece comes before the second.

blocks.note: a scar is a mark on the skin
f = female; the ’s just makes the surface read

annotation.surface: A woman has a mark on her neck, which she covers up.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a scar on a woman's neck; the break falls after 'female’s', which is just F. A scarf is exactly what might cover a scar there.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: a scarf is a strip of cloth wrapped around the neck, covering it.

entries.clue: Nobleman appointed to host king (4)

indicatorNotes.to host: A host takes guests into their home, so this word takes the next piece inside it.

blocks.note: due = appointed, as in 'at the due time'
K = king, as in chess; goes inside DUE

annotation.surface: A lord is designated to entertain the king.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Appointed' seems to be about a nobleman's role; it gives DUE, as in the appointed or due hour.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: in the British peerage the duke is the highest rank of nobleman.

entries.clue: Finished deliveries (4)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Deliveries' is plural because the answer is a set of six balls.

blocks.note: the sense of done, ended: 'the game is finished'
cricket: a delivery is one ball bowled, and the answer is a set of six of them

annotation.surface: The deliveries are finished; the parcels have all gone out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' reads as parcels; in cricket, a delivery is one ball bowled, and six of them make an over.
annotation.definitionFit: A double definition: 'it's over' means finished, and in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled.

entries.clue: Public square is place jazzman used now and again (5)

indicatorNotes.used now and again: Used now and again means used only some of the time, at intervals, so take every other letter.

blocks.note: Pl. is the street-name abbreviation for Place
every second letter of jAzZmAn

annotation.surface: A town square is where a jazz musician plays from time to time.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a busker in a square; 'place' looks like a synonym for square but is the address abbreviation PL.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym borrowed from Spanish: a plaza is an open square in a town, used by the public.

entries.clue: Five soldiers in gamble split up (7)

indicatorNotes.in: In means inside, so the pieces before it go inside the word after it.

blocks.note: V = five in Roman numerals
OR = other ranks, ordinary soldiers
to dice = to gamble; it is split to hold V and OR

annotation.surface: Five soldiers gambling together fall out and go their separate ways.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Split up' sounds like the soldiers scattering; it is the definition, a verb for ending a marriage.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiomatic synonym: couples who split up have separated, and divorcing is the legal form of it.

entries.clue: Clearly describe part of fish seen in Scottish river (6)

indicatorNotes.seen in: Something seen in a river is inside it, so this piece goes inside the river's name.

blocks.note: a fin is part of a fish; goes inside the river
the Dee flows through Aberdeenshire to Aberdeen

annotation.surface: A request to describe clearly the bit of a fish spotted in a Scottish river.
annotation.walkthrough: The angling surface hides the definition at the front, where 'Clearly describe' looks like an instruction to the solver; the Dee is a common crossword river.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to define is to set out exactly what something is, which is describing it clearly.

entries.clue: Ruffled young mare carrying queen (6)

indicatorNotes.carrying: A horse carrying a rider holds her on its back, so this word holds the next piece inside it.

blocks.note: a filly is a young female horse; it holds R
R = Regina, Latin for queen; goes inside FILLY

annotation.surface: A flustered young horse gives the queen a ride.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ruffled' looks like the mare's mood, flustered; it means trimmed with ruffles.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in dressmaking: ruffles and frills are the same gathered trim, so ruffled cloth is frilly.
